source_title: US approves $3 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
source_excerpt:
Patriot missiles are crucial to counter damaging ballistic missiles. ( AP: Sebastian Apel/US Department of Defense )
The US State Department has approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $US 2.1 billion ($3 billion).
It comes amid Ukraine's urgent calls for more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves of missiles Russia's military fires at the country.
Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors, with Pentagon negotiators ⁠pressing contractors to move quickly.
The United States has approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $US2.1 billion ($3 billion) in what would be one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since the start of the second Trump administration.
The US State Department made the announcement on Friday, local time, amid Ukraine's urgent calls for more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves of missiles Russia's military fires at the country.
The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.
Delayed missile deliveries have ‌added ⁠to Ukraine's tensions with the US after President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for Kyiv's unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy (left) and Donald Trump at the UN General Assembly in September. ( AP: Julia Demaree Nikhinson )
On Thursday, a Russian drone strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform in the Ukrainian ‌city of Dnipro, while five died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a missile strike killed one person in Kyiv, officials said.
Mr Zelenskyy said this week that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for the US to sign off on critical ​missile supplies, as Russia stepped up attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure.
But despite Ukraine's urgency, it will likely not receive the missile interceptors quickly.
Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles — which are yet to be manufactured — are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
One of the people said Ukraine's Ministry of Defence is encouraging the Pentagon to bring forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the US arsenal and backfilling with the new Patriot interceptors.
Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called US JUMPSTART, along with national funds financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan, the State Department said in a statement.
Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, with the capital Kyiv coming under fire. ( Reuters: Valentyn Ogirenko )
The program uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defence following Russia's invasion, according to a Pentagon website.
The JUMPSTART program was used in August to buy 3,350 air-launched cruise missiles worth $US825 million ($1.17 billion) made by Zone 5 Technologies and CoAspire.
Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.
The US ‌has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defence and precision-guided weapons.
In July, the US Army awarded Lockheed a contract worth up to $US58.6 billion ($83 billion) to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.
Lockheed has said that deal would allow it to follow through on a promise to triple PAC-3 MSE production capacity ​by the end of ​2030 and increase jobs ⁠at its Camden, Arkansas, plant by 50 per cent to about 1,850 from 1,200.
Lockheed previously announced Patriot PAC-3 missile interceptor production would go to 2,000 units ​annually.
Pentagon negotiators are ⁠pressing contractors to move much faster, with tentative production agreements struck this year at the centre of ​efforts to increase missile output.
